title: Add a Drain Line
summary: Plan and rough in a new drain for a bathroom sink, kitchen or bar sink, washer standpipe or utility sink: a proper P-trap, a vented trap arm, a sloped drain and a correct tie-in to the existing drain, tested and inspected before the walls close.
safety: Drains carry sewage: wear gloves and glasses, and make sure nobody uses fixtures upstream while a drain is open. Turn off power to walls you open and check for wires before cutting or drilling. Right-angle drills with large bits kick hard; brace them. Primer and cement are flammable with strong fumes: ventilate, no flames. Support heavy cast iron before cutting.
pro: New drains usually need a permit and inspection, and some areas require a licensed plumber. Call a plumber for cast iron or galvanized tie-ins, drains under a concrete slab, any work on the main stack or building drain, long or complicated runs, wet-vent designs, and anything the inspector flags.

tools.n: Tape measure, pencil, marker
tools.w: For the route, the stub-out height and every pipe cut.

tools.n: Torpedo level and a 2 ft or 4 ft level
tools.w: Checks the 1/4" per foot slope and plumb vents.

tools.n: Stud finder and flashlight
tools.w: Finds framing; the light lets you look into cavities before cutting.

tools.n: Non-contact voltage tester
tools.w: Checks for live wires before you cut drywall or drill.

tools.n: Drywall jab saw and utility knife
tools.w: Opens the wall and ceiling for access.

tools.n: PVC saw or hacksaw, plus a miter box
tools.w: Square cuts on new pipe. A wobbly cut won't seat fully in a fitting.

tools.n: Reciprocating saw with a fine-tooth blade
tools.w: Cuts the existing drain in tight spaces.

tools.n: Deburring tool or utility knife, and sandpaper
tools.w: Removes burrs that catch hair and debris and chamfers the end so it slides in.

tools.n: Heavy-duty right-angle drill (1/2" chuck)
tools.w: Large bits bind hard; a right-angle drill fits between joists and controls the kick. Hold it with both hands.

tools.n: Hole saw or self-feed bit, {{a.fixture==='washer'?'2-5/8"':'2-1/8"'}} for the drain, 2-1/8" for a 1-1/2" vent
tools.w: Slightly larger than the pipe's outside diameter so it slides through and can move with temperature.

tools.w: The clean way to cut cast iron. A grinder works but throws sparks and dust.

tools.n: Riser clamps sized to the stack (2)
tools.w: Hold a vertical cast iron stack up above and below the cut.

tools.w: DWV is drain-waste-vent pipe. Don't use thin-wall sewer pipe indoors.

tools.w: Vent pipe for one fixture is usually 1-1/4" or 1-1/2"; 1-1/2" is the safe common choice. Check local code.

steps.t: See how a drain system works
steps.idea: Every fixture needs a trap to block sewer gas, a sloped pipe to carry water, and a vent so the trap can't be sucked dry.
steps.b:
1. Look under an existing sink. Find the U-shaped trap. It always holds a few inches of water: that's the seal that blocks sewer gas.
  2. Follow the pipe from the trap into the wall. That level pipe is the trap arm.
  3. Inside the wall the arm meets a fitting: one pipe goes down (the drain) and one goes up (the vent).
  4. The vent joins other vents and leaves through the roof. Go outside and look for the pipe sticking out of the roof.
  5. The drain joins the stack, a big vertical pipe (often 3" or 4") that runs down to the building drain and the sewer or septic.
  6. Your new {{a.fixture==='bath'?'bathroom sink':a.fixture==='kitchen'?'kitchen or bar sink':a.fixture==='washer'?'washer standpipe':'utility sink'}} needs every piece of this: trap, trap arm, vent and a drain that ties into the system.
faq: What happens if I skip the vent?
The trap gets siphoned dry, so you smell sewer gas. You also get gurgling and slow drains. Unvented drains fail inspection.
Is a gurgling drain already a vent problem?
Often, yes: a blocked roof vent or an unvented fixture. Fix that before adding more fixtures to the line.

steps.t: Know the pipe size for your fixture
steps.idea: Each fixture has a minimum trap and drain size; never step down in size as you go downstream.
steps.b:
1. Your fixture: {{a.fixture==='bath'?'bathroom sink':a.fixture==='kitchen'?'kitchen or bar sink':a.fixture==='washer'?'washer standpipe':'utility sink'}}. Typical trap size: {{a.fixture==='bath'?'1-1/4"':a.fixture==='washer'?'2"':'1-1/2"'}}. Typical drain and trap arm: {{a.fixture==='washer'?'2"':'1-1/2"'}}.
  2. Bathroom sinks usually use a 1-1/4" trap, but the arm in the wall is commonly 1-1/2", which is easier to find and flows better.
  3. Washer standpipes need a 2" trap and 2" drain. A washer dumps water fast, and a smaller pipe overflows.
  4. Kitchen, bar and utility sinks: 1-1/2" trap and drain. Some codes or plumbers use 2" for kitchens.
  5. The new branch can join a bigger pipe, but never a smaller one.
  6. Confirm the sizes with your building department when you ask about the permit.
faq: Can I tie a washer into a 1-1/2" sink drain?
Usually not. A washer needs a 2" drain, and it can overflow the sink if they share a small line. Ask your inspector.
What does 'nominal size' mean?
The name, roughly the inside size. 1-1/2" PVC is about 1.9" outside. Bits, couplings and hangers go by the nominal size.

steps.t: Learn the trap arm and slope rules
steps.idea: The trap must reach its vent within a short distance, on a steady downhill slope, through a P-trap you can get to.
steps.b:
1. Measure from the trap to the vent fitting. That distance is the trap arm, and it has a limit. For your {{a.fixture==='washer'?'2"':'1-1/2"'}} arm it is about {{c.armIPC}} ft in areas using the IPC or IRC and about {{c.armUPC}} in UPC areas. Your local code decides.
  2. The vent must connect within that distance. If the old vent is farther away, you need a new vent (or an AAV where allowed).
  3. Slope the trap arm and drain 1/4" per foot, downhill toward the stack.
  4. Don't let the arm drop so much that the vent opening ends up below the trap's weir (the lip where water spills out of the trap).
  5. Use a P-trap only. S-traps, drum traps and "bell" traps are not allowed.
  6. The trap must stay reachable: under a cabinet or behind an access panel, never sealed in a wall.
faq: Why is there a maximum length?
A long, sloped arm can fill completely with water as it drains and siphon the trap. A short arm and a nearby vent stop that.
Can I add a second trap to be safe?
No. Double trapping is not allowed: it causes an air lock and slow drains.

steps.t: Stop: get the drain located first
steps.idea: If you can't find a drain nearby, the plan needs a plumber before any cutting.
steps.stop: A far or unknown drain usually means a long run, a new vent, or breaking a concrete slab. Have a licensed plumber design the route (and give you a quote) before you buy anything.
steps.b:
1. Look below the new location: basement ceiling or crawlspace. Is there a drain pipe within a few feet?
  2. Look for the main stack: it often sits behind a toilet wall or in a basement corner.
  3. On a slab foundation, drains are under the concrete. Tying in means cutting and digging the slab: that's pro work.
  4. Call a plumber for a route plan. Ask what you can do yourself (opening walls, patching) to save money.
  5. Once you know where the drain is and it's close, change your answer on the Start tab and continue.
faq: Could I use a pump instead?
Yes, a drain pump (a sink or laundry pump box) can lift water up to a drain. It still needs a vent, a permit and a check valve; ask a plumber.

steps.t: Stop: metal drains lean to a pro
steps.idea: Cast iron and galvanized drains are heavy, brittle or rusted, and cutting them can break joints you can't see.
steps.stop: {{a.material==='galv'?'Old galvanized drains are often rusted thin inside and can crumble when cut. Have a plumber replace that section with PVC or ABS and install the tie-in fitting.':'Cutting a cast iron stack is heavy, hazardous work. A plumber is strongly recommended for the tie-in. If you do it, follow the cast iron step exactly and get help.'}}
steps.b:
1. Identify the pipe: cast iron is dark, heavy and rings when tapped; joints are bulging hubs or rubber no-hub bands. Galvanized steel is gray with threaded joints.
  2. Look for rust, cracks or weeping joints. A drain that's already failing is a replacement job, not a tie-in.
  3. Get a plumber's quote for just the tie-in. You can often do the rest (new pipe, vent, fixture) and have the plumber connect it.
  4. Ask the inspector whether a homeowner may do this part in your area.
faq: Can I use a rubber coupling right on cast iron?
Yes, with a heavy-duty shielded coupling made for cast iron to plastic. The hard part is cutting and supporting the old pipe, not the coupling.

steps.idea: Decide how the new trap gets air: through a pipe to an existing vent, or through an AAV where the code allows it.
steps.b:
1. Find the nearest existing vent: from the attic, from the fixture's wall, or by following the pipes up from the basement.
  2. Tie into an existing vent: run a new dry vent straight up from the vent tee. Keep it vertical until it's above the fixture's flood rim (often at least 6" above, check code), then slope it slightly back toward the drain as it runs over to the old vent.
  3. Air admittance valve (AAV): a one-way valve that lets air in. Many IPC/IRC areas allow one; many UPC areas restrict it. Ask your building department before you plan on it.
  4. An AAV must stay accessible and upright, sit above the trap arm by the maker's minimum (often 4"), and is never a replacement for the house's main vent through the roof.
  5. Your choice: {{a.vent==='existing'?'tie into an existing vent':a.vent==='aav'?'AAV, if your code allows it':'not sure yet'}}.
  6. {{a.vent==='unsure'?'Bring your sketch to the building department and ask which vent option they accept. Don\'t cut anything until you know.':'Write the plan on your sketch for the permit.'}}
steps.stop: {{a.vent==='unsure'?'Settle the vent before you cut. A drain with no approved vent fails inspection and can let sewer gas into the house.':'Never use a horizontal dry vent below the flood rim. If the fixture backs up, the vent fills with waste and clogs.'}}
faq: Can I connect the vent into the drain of another fixture?
Not into a drain below. A vent must join another vent (dry), above the flood rim of the highest fixture it serves, unless your code allows a special wet-vent design. That's plumber design work.
Can an AAV go inside the wall?
Only in a ventilated box with an access grille. It must get air and you must be able to replace it.

steps.t: Pick the tie-in point and fitting
steps.idea: Join the old drain where it's big enough, downstream of the new fixture, with the right fitting for its direction.
steps.b:
1. Find a drain at least as big as your new pipe ({{a.fixture==='washer'?'2"':'1-1/2"'}} or larger), {{a.drain==='below'?'in the basement or crawlspace below':'in the wall near the fixture'}}.
  2. The tie-in must be lower than the new trap arm by enough for 1/4" per foot all the way.
  3. Pick a straight section with at least 8"-12" of clear pipe on each side, away from existing fittings, so the couplings fit.
  4. Don't tie a sink or washer into a toilet's short arm, or below a toilet into its own 3" drain without asking the inspector.
  5. Choose the fitting by direction: {{a.tiein==='vertical'?'vertical stack: a sanitary tee, branch coming in from the side':'horizontal drain: a wye with a 1/8 bend, or a combo wye, branch rolled up above the center line'}}.
  6. Never lay a sanitary tee on its back on a horizontal line.
  7. Existing pipe: {{a.material==='pvc'?'PVC':a.material==='abs'?'ABS':a.material==='cast'?'cast iron':'galvanized steel'}}. Measure its outside size and buy couplings for that size.
faq: How do I tell the size of the old drain?
Wrap a string around it and measure: about 6" around is 1-1/2", 7-1/2" is 2", 11" is 3" plastic. Cast iron is a little different; take the measurement to the store.
Why not a sanitary tee everywhere?
Its sharp turn is designed for water falling down. On a horizontal pipe, waste shoots straight into the opposite wall and backs up.

steps.t: Plan the route and the stub-out height
steps.idea: A short, steadily sloped route through framing you're allowed to drill, ending at the right height for the fixture.
steps.b:
1. Sketch the route from the fixture to the tie-in. Measure along the path, including up and down: {{a.run}} ft.
  2. Drop on the way: {{a.run}} ft at 1/4" per foot = {{frac(c.drop)}}. The tie-in must be at least that much lower than where the drain starts.
  3. Stub-out height: {{a.fixture==='bath'?'bathroom sinks are commonly 16"-20" to the center of the drain':a.fixture==='kitchen'?'kitchen and bar sinks are commonly 15"-18"; lower if a disposal is going in':a.fixture==='washer'?'washer trap commonly 6"-18" above the floor, standpipe top 18"-42" above the trap weir (30" max in UPC areas); a recessed washer box puts the top around 42"-48"':'utility sinks vary, often 12"-18"; read the tub\'s spec sheet'}}. The fixture's spec sheet wins.
  4. Count the joists or studs you'll drill: {{a.holes}}. Check each against the drilling limits.
  5. Avoid exterior walls in cold climates, and load-bearing 2x4 walls for a horizontal run.
  6. Plan a cleanout where the inspector wants one, often at the upper end of a long horizontal run or where bends add up.
faq: The route crosses the joists. Do I drill all of them?
Often you can hang the pipe below the joists in a basement instead. That keeps the slope easy and skips drilling.
What if the drop is more than I have room for?
Shorten the route, tie in lower, or ask a plumber. Never flatten the slope to make it fit.

steps.idea: New drains are permit work almost everywhere, and the inspection is your proof the system is safe.
steps.b:
1. Call or visit your city or county building department. Ask: "I'm adding a drain for a {{a.fixture==='bath'?'bathroom sink':a.fixture==='kitchen'?'kitchen or bar sink':a.fixture==='washer'?'washer standpipe':'utility sink'}} and tying into an existing drain. Do I need a plumbing permit? Can a homeowner pull it?"
  2. Ask which code they use (IPC, IRC or UPC) and the local limits: trap arm length, vent options (AAV allowed?), standpipe height, and cleanouts.
  3. Ask what test they want (water test or air test) and when to call for inspection: usually rough-in before walls close, then final.
  4. Bring your sketch: fixture, pipe sizes, route, slope, vent and tie-in point.
  5. Apply and wait for approval before cutting into the existing drain.
steps.stop: If your area requires a licensed plumber for drain work, hire one. Unpermitted drain work can cause problems with insurance claims and home sales, and a bad drain can leak sewage inside walls.
faq: Is a laundry standpipe really permit work?
In most areas, yes: it is a new fixture drain with a trap and vent.
Will the inspector help me plan?
Many will answer code questions. They won't design it for you, but they'll tell you what they need to see.

steps.idea: Match the new pipe to your plan and the old pipe, and buy extra fittings to return.
steps.b:
1. Drain pipe: {{c.drainSticks}} x 10 ft of {{a.fixture==='washer'?'2"':'1-1/2"'}} Schedule 40 {{a.material==='abs'?'ABS':'PVC'}} DWV ({{c.drainLen}} ft needed).
  2. Vent pipe: {{a.vent==='aav'?'a short piece of 1-1/2" for the AAV riser':c.ventSticks+' x 10 ft of 1-1/2"'}}.
  3. Fittings: about {{c.fit}} in all (tie-in, vent tee, bends, couplings, trap adapter, cleanout). Buy two or three spare bends and couplings; return what you don't use.
  4. Look for "DWV" printed on fittings. Pressure fittings have tight turns that don't belong on drains.
  5. Shielded couplings sized to the old pipe: {{a.material==='cast'?'heavy-duty, made for cast iron to plastic':'match the outside size of the existing pipe'}}.
  6. {{a.material==='abs'?'Your old drain is ABS: use ABS pipe and ABS cement, or a shielded coupling where ABS meets PVC. Don\'t glue ABS to PVC unless your code allows transition cement.':'Primer and cement for PVC.'}}
  7. Also: {{c.hangers}} hangers, {{c.plates}} nail plates, a test cap and test plug.
faq: Foam core or solid PVC?
Both are sold as Schedule 40 DWV and many codes accept both for drains. Solid wall is quieter and stronger. Check with your inspector.

steps.idea: Make enough access to work safely and see what's inside before any drilling.
steps.b:
1. Turn off the breaker for outlets and lights on the wall you're opening. Check outlets with the voltage tester.
  2. Mark the studs. Cut a test hole about 4" square and look inside with a flashlight for wires, pipes and ducts.
  3. Cut the opening between studs, from the stub-out height down to the floor, or the ceiling strip under the route.
  4. Keep drywall pieces if you want to reuse them.
  5. Move insulation aside or bag it.
steps.stop: If you find wiring in the path, reroute the pipe or have an electrician move it. Never drill blind through a wall or floor.
faq: How big should the hole be?
Big enough for your hands and a drill: usually one stud bay wide and from the floor to a few inches above the stub-out.

steps.idea: Holes go where the wood can spare them, and each joist hole steps down to keep the slope.
steps.b:
1. Snap a sloped line along the joists or studs: start at the stub-out height and drop 1/4" per foot.
  2. Mark each hole center on that line. Check: middle of the joist, not within 2" of the top or bottom, no bigger than 1/3 of the depth.
  3. Studs: hole no bigger than 40% of the stud width in a bearing wall (60% in a non-bearing wall), at least 5/8" from either edge.
  4. Brace the right-angle drill with its side handle. Drill at low speed and let the bit cut.
  5. Check each hole lines up: slide a length of pipe through as you go.
  6. Holes through top or bottom plates: note them for fire caulk later.
steps.stop: Right-angle drills with big bits kick hard when they bind. Keep both hands on the drill, brace the handle against a stud, and never stand where the handle can swing into you. Don't cut I-joists, trusses or beams outside the maker's rules.
faq: My hole has to be bigger than the limit.
Hang the pipe below the joists, re-route, add a stud shoe where your code allows, or fur out the wall. Never weaken a load-bearing member to fit a pipe.

steps.idea: The vent tee, trap arm and stub-out set the height and the vent for the whole job.
steps.b:
1. Set the sanitary tee in the wall: run up (vent), run down (drain), and the curved branch facing the fixture.
  2. {{a.fixture==='washer'?'Mount the washer box or set the trap so its weir is 6"-18" above the floor (or per your code). Glue the 2" trap below the box and connect its outlet to the tee.':'Cut a short stub from the tee\'s branch out through the wall. Its center should be at the planned stub-out height.'}}
  3. Check the arm slope: 1/4" per foot downhill toward the tee.
  4. Check the distance from the trap to the tee is within your trap arm limit (about {{c.armIPC}} ft IPC/IRC, {{c.armUPC}} UPC).
  5. Fasten the tee to a block or strap so it can't move when you push the trap on later.
  6. Dry-fit only for now. Mark each joint with a line across pipe and fitting so you can glue it in the same position.
faq: Which way does the san tee face?
The curved inlet points at the fixture and curves down. If you can read the arrow cast on it, it points in the flow direction (down).

steps.t: Run the drain with slope and hangers
steps.idea: Steady downhill slope with support every few feet carries waste without settling.
steps.b:
1. Measure and cut each piece, dry-fit and mark it.
  2. Use long-sweep bends or two 1/8 bends for turns from horizontal to horizontal or vertical to horizontal.
  3. Check slope on every horizontal piece: 1/4" per foot. No flat spots, no high spots.
  4. Hang the pipe at least every 4 ft, and near each fitting. Snug, not pinching.
  5. Put in the cleanout where the inspector wants it, facing where you can get a snake in.
  6. Stop the run a few inches short of the tie-in. You'll connect it last.
faq: Can I use regular 90 elbows?
A tight (short) 1/4 bend is only for turning from horizontal to vertical (water going down). For turns that flow sideways or from vertical to horizontal, use long sweeps or two 45s.
Steeper is better, right?
Steeper is usually fine, but it uses up your height. Aim for 1/4" per foot and stay consistent.

steps.idea: The vent goes straight up from the tee until it's above the flood rim, then over to the existing vent.
steps.b:
1. Run 1-1/2" pipe straight up from the top of the vent tee.
  2. Keep it vertical until it's above the fixture's flood rim (the top edge of the sink or standpipe), at least 6" above where your code requires.
  3. Turn it over toward the existing vent with long sweeps. Slope horizontal sections slightly back toward the drain so condensation drains away.
  4. Plan to join the existing vent with a sanitary tee (inverted, so it catches air) or a wye. You'll cut in during the tie-in.
  5. Use shielded couplings to close the cut in the old vent, the same way as on the drain.
  6. Through ceilings and top plates: drill the plate, keep the hole within limits, and fire caulk later.
steps.stop: {{a.vent==='unsure'?'You marked the vent plan as not sure. Don\'t build it until your inspector approves the plan.':'Don\'t join a vent into a drain pipe below the flood rim, and don\'t lay a dry vent flat below it.'}}
faq: How do I know the old pipe is a vent and not a drain?
Trace it: a vent goes up to the roof with no fixtures above it. Run water upstairs and listen. If water runs through it, it's a drain.

steps.idea: The AAV sits upright on a short riser above the trap arm, where it gets air and can be replaced.
steps.b:
1. Glue a short vertical riser into the top of the vent tee.
  2. Cut it so the bottom of the AAV sits at least the maker's minimum above the trap arm (often 4"). Higher is fine.
  3. Keep it plumb: most AAVs must be within about 15° of vertical. Check with the torpedo level.
  4. Screw the AAV on (threaded adapter) or push it on as the maker says. Don't glue the valve itself, so it can be replaced.
  5. Inside a cabinet it's already accessible. In a wall, use an AAV box with an access grille.
  6. Keep it out of insulation and attics where it can freeze unless the maker allows it.
faq: Can I add AAVs everywhere instead of venting?
No. The house must keep at least one vent open to the roof, and codes limit where AAVs go.

steps.idea: Primer and cement weld the plastic. A joint that isn't pushed in fully or turned leaks.
steps.b:
1. Open a window or run a fan. Primer and cement fumes are strong and flammable: no flames or smoking.
  2. Take one joint apart at a time. Wipe both parts clean and dry.
  3. {{a.material==='abs'?'Brush ABS cement on the pipe end and inside the fitting.':'Brush purple primer on the pipe end and inside the fitting. While wet, brush on PVC cement.'}}
  4. Push the pipe fully in with a quarter turn, lining up your marks. Hold 30 seconds; it pushes back.
  5. Wipe extra cement. Work from the fixture toward the tie-in.
  6. Check slope and hangers again once it's all glued.
faq: I glued one wrong.
Cut it out and use a new fitting with couplings. Glued joints can't be pulled apart.
Do I need primer on ABS?
Usually no. Use ABS cement made for DWV. Some areas require a cleaner; ask.

steps.t: Stop the water going down the drain
steps.idea: Nobody upstream may run water while the old drain is open.
steps.b:
1. Find every fixture that drains through the pipe you'll cut: sinks, tubs, toilets, washer upstairs.
  2. Tell everyone at home. Tape a note on each fixture: "Don't use: drain open."
  3. Turn off the washer and dishwasher if they drain here.
  4. Put a bucket and rags under the cut point. Wear gloves and glasses.
  5. Expect some dirty water and smell. Keep a fan running.
steps.stop: An open drain plus a flushed toilet upstairs sends sewage onto you and the floor. Make sure everyone knows.

steps.t: Support and cut the plastic drain
steps.idea: Hold the old pipe up on both sides, then cut out a gap that fits the new fitting.
steps.b:
1. Add a hanger or strap on both sides of the cut, within about a foot, so the pipe can't sag or drop.
  2. Hold the new fitting next to the pipe. Mark the cut length: the fitting's length plus about 1/4" for the couplings' center stops, or as the coupling maker says.
  3. Cut square with the saw. Keep the blade straight; the cut ends must meet the coupling's stop.
  4. Clean off burrs and wipe the ends dry.
  5. If the pipe is vertical, cut the bottom first, then the top, and support the section above before the second cut.
faq: Can I glue the new fitting in instead?
If the pipe can flex enough, yes, using a repair coupling (slip coupling, no inner stop) on one side. Shielded couplings are easier on a fixed pipe.
Water keeps trickling out.
Something upstream is still draining. Find it, or plug the upstream end with a rag or test ball while you work.

steps.idea: Clamp the stack above and below, then cut it square with a snap cutter.
steps.stop: Cast iron is heavy and brittle. If the stack isn't clamped above and below, it can drop when cut, break joints elsewhere, and injure you. Hire a plumber if you're unsure.
steps.b:
1. Install a riser clamp above the cut, resting on the floor framing. On a vertical stack, add one below the cut too.
  2. Mark the cut: fitting length plus the coupling's stops.
  3. Wrap the snap cutter chain around the pipe at the first mark. Pump the handle until the pipe snaps cleanly.
  4. Repeat at the second mark. Have a helper hold the section that comes out.
  5. Check the ends: square, not cracked. Wire brush them clean.
  6. Use heavy-duty shielded couplings made for cast iron to plastic.
faq: Can I use a grinder?
It works but throws sparks and lots of dust, and the cut is slower. A rented snap cutter is cleaner and safer.

steps.idea: The new fitting fills the gap; the couplings seal it to the old pipe.
steps.b:
1. {{a.material==='galv'?'Your plumber replaces the rusty galvanized section and leaves this fitting in place. Check it matches your plan, then skip to connecting the new branch.':'Slide a shielded coupling onto each cut end, rubber sleeve first.'}}
  2. Set the fitting in the gap. Branch facing your new line: {{a.tiein==='vertical'?'sanitary tee on the stack, branch in from the side':'wye pointing downstream, branch rolled up at or above the center line'}}.
  3. Center each coupling over its joint. Tighten the band clamps evenly to the torque on the coupling (often 60 inch-pounds; a torque wrench or preset T-handle helps).
  4. Connect your new branch to the fitting: glue it or use another coupling.
  5. Check the slope from the fixture to here one last time.
  6. Leave the upstream fixtures off until the test is done.
faq: Do I need a torque wrench?
Over-tightening cuts the rubber; under-tightening leaks. A 5/16" nut driver torque tool for no-hub couplings is cheap and removes the guesswork.

steps.idea: Fill the new piping with water and prove no joint leaks before the walls close.
steps.b:
1. Wait for the cement to cure as the can says before testing. Cold weather takes longer.
  2. Cap the stub-out with a test cap.
  3. Plug the new branch at the tie-in with a test ball or plug, so test water can't escape into the old drain.
  4. Fill the new piping with a hose or bucket through the top of the vent until it's full to the highest point.
  5. Mark the water level. Wait 15 minutes (or what your inspector asks). The level must not drop.
  6. Walk every joint with a dry paper towel. Release the water slowly into a bucket afterward.
steps.stop: If the level drops, find the leak and fix it now. A leaking drain in a closed wall rots framing and grows mold before you notice.
faq: My inspector wants an air test.
That uses plugs and a gauge at 5 psi. Ask them exactly what they want; some accept a water test for a small branch.
I can't fill to the top of the vent.
Fill as high as you can and tell the inspector. With an AAV, fill to just below the valve.

steps.idea: The inspector checks sizes, slope, venting and the test before anything gets covered.
steps.b:
1. Call for the rough-in inspection with the walls and ceiling still open.
  2. Leave everything visible: the tie-in, the vent, hangers, nail plate spots, cleanout.
  3. Have the test ready if they want to watch it.
  4. Fix anything the inspector flags. If it involves the stack, slab or main drain, call a plumber.
  5. Keep the signed inspection card.
faq: What do inspectors flag most?
Wrong fittings on horizontal lines, flat or back-sloped pipe, long trap arms, missing cleanouts, and unsupported pipe.

steps.idea: Plates stop future screws; fire caulk restores the fire block; then the wall goes back.
steps.b:
1. Nail a steel plate on the stud face wherever the pipe is within 1-1/4" of the edge. In 2x4 and most 2x6 walls, that's every stud you drilled.
  2. Fill holes through top and bottom plates with fire-rated caulk.
  3. Put insulation back.
  4. Patch the drywall. Leave an access panel if a cleanout or AAV is in the wall.
faq: Do I need an access panel?
Yes for a cleanout, an AAV in the wall or any slip-joint fitting. Those must stay reachable.

steps.idea: The trap connects the fixture to the stub-out and holds the water seal.
steps.b:
1. {{a.fixture==='washer'?'Set the washer drain hose into the standpipe about 6"-8" deep, loose, never sealed or taped. Strap it so it can\'t jump out.':'Glue the trap adapter onto the stub-out. Install the fixture per its instructions.'}}
  2. {{a.fixture==='washer'?'Check the standpipe top is above the washer\'s flood level and within the code height.':'Connect the tailpiece, trap and trap arm. Slip nuts go on first, then beveled washers with the bevel facing the joint.'}}
  3. {{a.fixture==='washer'?'Hand-tighten any washer box valves and check for drips.':'Hand-tighten slip nuts, then about a quarter turn more with pliers. Don\'t crush the plastic.'}}
  4. The trap must be a P-trap, level side to side, with no long dip or second trap.
faq: The trap doesn't line up with the stub-out.
Trap arms can be cut shorter or swiveled. If it's off by more than an inch or two, add a short piece; don't stretch slip joints.

steps.idea: Run lots of water and watch every joint and listen for gurgling.
steps.b:
1. Remove all test plugs and caps. Tell the household the drains are back on.
  2. {{a.fixture==='washer'?'Run a full washer drain cycle and watch the standpipe top. No overflow, no bubbling back.':'Fill the sink, then pull the plug. Watch under it with a flashlight.'}}
  3. Listen: gurgling means a vent problem. The trap should stay full afterward.
  4. Check the tie-in and every joint you can reach for drips with a dry paper towel.
  5. Check again the next day.
  6. Call for the final inspection if your permit needs one.
steps.stop: If it gurgles, drains slowly or smells like sewer gas, the vent isn't working or the slope is wrong. Don't just live with it: have a plumber look.
faq: The trap smells after a few weeks of no use.
The water evaporated. Run water monthly in rarely used drains or add a few drops of mineral oil.

days.t: Learn, plan and apply for the permit

days.wait: cement cure overnight is a good idea

glueHelp.t: Prime and glue plastic drain pipe
glueHelp.b:
1. Square cut, deburred, chamfered.
  2. Dry-fit and mark across the joint.
  3. PVC: purple primer on pipe and socket, then cement while wet. ABS: ABS cement only.
  4. Push fully home with a 1/4 turn to the mark.
  5. Hold 30 seconds. Wipe extra.

slopeHelp.b:
1. Set the level on the pipe.
  2. Lift the low end until the bubble centers.
  3. The gap should be 1/4" per foot of level: 1/4" under a 1 ft torpedo, 1" under a 4 ft level.
  4. Many torpedo levels have a 1/4" slope line on the vial.

drillHelp.b:
1. Joists: middle, 2" from edges, max 1/3 depth.
  2. Studs: 40% of width (bearing), 60% (non-bearing), 5/8" from edges.
  3. Never notch for a drain.
  4. Engineered lumber: maker's chart only.
  5. Plate any stud face where the pipe is within 1-1/4".

cutHelp.b:
1. Mark all the way around (wrap a strip of paper as a guide).
  2. Use a miter box or saw slowly while turning the pipe.
  3. Remove burrs inside and out; chamfer the outside edge slightly.
  4. Dry-fit: the pipe must reach the fitting's stop.

vent.title: What a vent does
vent.cap: Without a vent, draining water pulls a vacuum behind it and siphons the trap. An empty trap lets sewer gas into the room. Gurgling and slow drains are the warning signs.

glossary: DWV
Drain-waste-vent: the pipe and fittings made for drains and vents, with gentle turns. Different from pressure fittings.
Trap
The U-shaped pipe under a fixture that holds water to block sewer gas. A P-trap is the allowed shape.
Trap weir
The lip inside the trap where water spills over into the trap arm. It sets the trap's water level.
Trap arm
The pipe from the trap to the vent fitting. Its length is limited by code.
Vent
A pipe that lets air into the drain so traps aren't siphoned. It ends at the roof or an approved AAV.
Dry vent
A vent pipe that never carries water.
Flood rim
The top edge of a fixture, where water would spill over if it filled up.
AAV
Air admittance valve: a one-way valve that lets air into a drain but not gas out. Allowed only where local code permits.
Stack
A large vertical drain pipe that collects branches and continues up as a vent through the roof.
Sanitary tee
A tee with a curved inlet, for joining a horizontal branch into a vertical pipe.
Wye
A Y-shaped fitting for joining branches into horizontal drains. Used with a 1/8 bend; a combo wye has the bend built in.
1/8 bend / 1/4 bend
45° and 90° drain fittings. Long-sweep 1/4 bends turn more gently.
Shielded no-hub coupling
A rubber sleeve with a stainless steel band and clamps that joins pipe ends, including different materials.
Standpipe
The vertical pipe a washer hose drains into, with a trap at its base.
Stub-out
The short pipe coming out of the wall where the fixture connects.
Cleanout
A removable plug that gives a drain snake access to the pipe.
S-trap
An old trap shape that drops straight down after the bend. It siphons itself and isn't allowed.
IPC / IRC / UPC
The model plumbing codes most US areas adopt. Your local version and amendments are what count.
